prize_parts.citation: for the invention and development of the optical lattice clock

statement.case_for: I opened with the Higgs boson discovery first, but the colleagues' arguments and my own attribution test lead me to move the optical lattice clock to the head of my list. It is the only shortlisted candidate that every member placed in the top three, and three members placed it first. The invention is conceptually clear (the magic-wavelength lattice that removes the light shift), it has been realised by many independent laboratories at fractional uncertainties near 1e-18, and it underpins redefinition of the SI second, relativistic geodesy and laboratory tests of fundamental constants. As an experimentalist who builds instruments, I value that this is a measurement capability that nature did not hand us but that someone had to invent and then drive to its systematic limit. The credit also divides cleanly: Katori proposed and first demonstrated the concept, and Ye drove the strontium clock to record accuracy and many-body regimes. Two names fit the three-person statute without forcing arbitrary exclusions.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is overlap with earlier timekeeping and precision-spectroscopy recognition (the 2005 frequency comb prize and the 2012 prize for control of single quantum systems, including ion-clock groundwork). A fair reading is that the lattice clock is a distinct invention, yet the committee may judge that the field has been well served already. There is also the unresolved question of credit to other clock groups and technology contributors (ultrastable lasers, the ion-clock lineage) who are not in the credited names. Finally, the redefinition of the second has not yet happened, so some of the promised fundamental-physics payoff is prospective, not realised. Against that, the Higgs discovery remains the most consequential outstanding experimental result in particle physics, but any three-person credit for ATLAS and CMS necessarily omits deserving leaders, and I do not think its attribution problem is better resolved than the lattice clock's.

responses.point: Kroll ranked the optical lattice clock first as a landmark for experimental atomic physics, while noting uncertainty about whether it is sufficiently distinct from the 2005 and 2012 prizes and that his priority details rest on recollection.
responses.response: I agree on the central merit and I take the overlap worry seriously, but I would separate the instrument from the earlier prizes. The 2005 award recognised the comb as a ruler for optical frequencies and the 2012 award recognised control of individual quantum systems; the lattice clock exploits many neutral atoms interrogated at a magic wavelength, which is a different route to the accuracy and stability, and the 1e-18 results come from that route. Where I qualify his view is on priority: I would want the committee's expert evaluation of Katori's 2001-2003 proposal and demonstration against parallel lattice-clock work before we fix the citation wording.

responses.point: Danielsson put the CMB acoustic-peak and precision mapping work first because it is a measurement supplied by nature on which much later cosmology rests, and treated the clock as a clear invention with a clear payoff in second place.
responses.response: I respect the argument that the CMB turned cosmology quantitative, and I do not dispute its maturity. My difficulty is attribution: five credited names with COBE-era, balloon, WMAP and Planck lines mean that any trio omits Planck or the theory of acoustic oscillations, and I see that as a more serious obstacle than the one facing the lattice clock. I would not rank it below the clock on scientific merit, but I do not see a three-person configuration we could defend today.

responses.point: Eriksson ranked topological insulators and the quantum spin Hall effect first, with the clock second, and flagged that the HgTe prediction by Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang falls outside the supplied names.
responses.response: I agree that the Kane-Mele Z2 classification is decisive and that Molenkamp's experiment gave the field its first confirmation. I disagree that the omission of Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang is a minor complication: they proposed the HgTe route that made the experiment possible, and a trio of Kane, Mele and Molenkamp would sever the chain between prediction and observation. That makes the topological configuration vulnerable in a way the two-name clock configuration is not, and I would keep it as a strong second-tier option rather than my lead.

responses.point: Lindroth ranked the clock first, arguing that Katori and Ye form a fair, coherent two-person configuration and asking whether credit between Katori's proposal and the later precision development is fairly split between only two.
responses.response: I share her view that Katori and Ye are the right pair, and I would answer her split question by noting that the two contributions are different in kind: Katori made the concept and first realisation, Ye made the performance and many-body regime that convinced the community. I would not support adding a third name only to fill the quota, since Hall and Hansch were honoured in 2005 and the remaining candidates for a third place have a weaker claim to the lattice-clock invention itself.

uncertainties: How the committee's expert evaluation weighs Katori's original proposal and early demonstration against parallel lattice-clock work, since our opening arguments rely on recollection.
Whether the overlap with the 2005 and 2012 prizes will be judged as a real obstacle or as a distinct invention.
Whether a Higgs configuration could be made defensible, given that any three names among the ATLAS and CMS leaders omit others with equal claims.
Whether the IceCube credit to Halzen and Karle is complete given AMANDA and Baikal precursors and the still-limited source identification.
statement.conflict_note: My profile records membership in the PAMELA, Fermi-LAT, PoGOLite/PoGO+ and XL-Calibur collaborations and a doctorate in accelerator-based particle physics at CERN. That is an astroparticle and particle-physics connection that bears on the IceCube neutrino candidate (B033) and the Higgs candidate (B054), which I list as alternatives, so I would flag it for a recusal discussion if either becomes the lead. No specific conflict is apparent for the optical lattice clock candidate (B048) from the provided profile.
